newsitem.title: USA: Alcatel, Hayes in high-speed modem pact.
newsitem.headline: Alcatel, Hayes in high-speed modem pact.

text.p: Alcatel Alsthom, the French telecom equipment group, said Monday it had teamed up with with U.S. modem maker Hayes Microcomputer Products Inc in a deal to develop high-speed Internet access equipment.

The two companies said Hayes would build consumer modems based on Asynchronous Digital Subscriber Line (ADSL) technology that would enable consumers, telecommuters and small business computer users to gain high-speed access to the Internet and interactive services such as corporate Intranets.
Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Hayes said it will develop, as the first in a series of collaborative products with Alcatel, an ADSL network interface card, or modem which fits inside a personal computer.

The Hayes modems would work with ADSL systems equipment Alcatel is building on behalf of a consortium of four U.S. Baby Bells, industry analysts said. The Hayes pact will help Alcatel meet upcoming deadlines on that project, they said.
The Alcatel ADSL contract, which was announced last September and carries an estimated value of $300 million, is considered the largest deal to date to supply ADSL equipment.
The Baby Bell group, known as the Joint Procurement Consortium (JPC), includes Ameritech Corp, BellSouth Corp, SBC Communications Inc and its recently acquired Pacific Telesis unit.

For example, SBC's Pacific Bell has said it is gearing up to use the ADSL system beginning in September in certain overloaded central office switches in California as a way to reduce growing data congestion on voice networks.
Daniel Briere, president of industry consulting firm TeleChoice Inc, and publisher of the ADSL Report, said the Hayes pact should help Alcatel meet its deadlines.

"The only question was whether Alcatel could deliver this on time," Briere said of Alactel's U.S. ADSL supply contract. "This deal gives Alcatel security that it can meet its delivery dates," he said.
Hayes will provide not only technology, but also the necessary consumer marketing and customer service focus that Alcatel Telecom, a supplier of large network systems, lacks.

"Alcatel needs to partner with someone like Hayes who can provide that," Briere said. Hayes is a pioneer in the consumer modem business, having developed many of the basic standards now widely used in personal computer modems.

Privately held Hayes, of Norcross, Ga., is staging a comeback after a brush with bankruptcy in 1994. The pact with Alcatel could help once again thrust it to center-stage in the emerging high-speed modem marketplace.
ADSL offers a low-cost method of high-speed data delivery because it uses existing telephone copper-wire phone networks.

The Alcatel/Hayes system permits data trasmission at up to eight megabits per second into homes or businesses, or 200 times faster than current 28.8 kilobit per second modems, the companies said. Signals from customer premises to phone networks travel at a slower speed of 640,000 bits per second.
Alcatel's decision to partner with Hayes has implications for other equipment suppliers.

Hayes modems use ADSL software from Aware Inc and semiconductor chipsets built by Analog Devices Inc, a different combination than that called for in Alcatel original ADSL plans, which envisioned building its ADSL modems around chips developed by an Alcatel-controlled company, Briere said.
Delays in carrying through on its internal development strategy may lead Alcatel to adopt Analog Devices/Aware as the underlying technology for its own ADSL equipment, he said.
Briere said Alcatel demonstrated pieces of its ADSL system at a telecom equipment trade show in New Orleans last week.
